en: An Explanation of the *Buddhabhāṣita-pratimā-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*,
translated and annotated by Gongbu Chabu, Chief of the Bureau of Tibetan Studies and Imperial Knight (*Yibin*),
who served as the Director of Translations for the Manchu and Mongolian Documents of the Grand Council of the Great Qing.
The Sūtra on the Proportions for Constructing Images, as Spoken by the Buddha. Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Together with all the bodhisattvas, śrāvaka disciples,
and the vast assembly of immeasurable followers— including humans, devas, nāgas, and spirits.
This was precisely when the World-Honored One,
having preached the Dharma for his mother,
was about to ascend to the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra paid homage to the Buddha and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One, you do not abide within this realm."
If there are virtuous people who cannot overcome their longing and yearning,
who desire to behold the World-Honored One,
and wish to create an image of him;
"What then is the method for doing so?
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, Śāriputra."
I shall now ascend briefly to the celestial realms;
before I have returned from there,
or even after manifesting my entry into nirvana without remainder, [this shall occur].
If there are virtuous persons who wish to contemplate and gaze upon [it], and who,
for the benefit of themselves and others, act as a field of merit;
Those who wish to create images must fashion them according to the rules for proportions;
such is the measurement of the Tathāgata’s body.
Its length and breadth are proportionate, like a nyagrodha tree,
reaching a full fathom in height.
Now, as for the proportions of his body's limbs and joints,
both vertical and horizontal measurements,
they begin from the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of his head.
I shall explain it to you in brief;
listen attentively and reflect upon it well, both in its extent and its breadth.
It is like a vertical crossbar.
Nyagrodha is the name of a tree.
It is a term from the Sanskrit language;
in Chinese it is called "wujie" (unjointed).
Its appearance is like that of the willow.
The height of this tree’s trunk is equal to the depth of the space between its surrounding drooping branches, whether measured vertically or horizontally.
The Buddha’s body is likewise:
the vertical measurement from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet is equal to the span of his two arms when stretched out horizontally.
The distance between the tips of the middle fingers of the two hands is as wide as a *vitasti*;
there is nothing that is not in proportion,
each reaching the full measure of one *vyāma* for oneself.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses (*gāthā*). *Gāthā* is a term from the Sanskrit language;
in the Chinese language, it is translated as "verse" (*jì*).
The meaning is detailed while the phrasing is concise;
it is easy for students to retain.
It is measured by the span of one's own fingers.
There are one hundred and twenty fingers [in height].
The uṣṇīṣa is four fingers high;
the hairline is likewise. This follows the measurement methods of the iconographic school that was professionally transmitted from the West.
A mote of dust;
the tip of a hair; a nit.
Mustard seeds and barley;
thereafter, it increases eightfold again.
One barley grain constitutes one small part (*aṃśa*).
Two barley grains laid side by side constitute one foot (*pāda*).
Four feet constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
Furthermore, it is said that the middle portion consists of twelve finger-breadths (*vitasti*).
That which is measured with the hand is called a *vitasti*.
In common parlance, it is called a *mahā-śakta* or a *mahā-bhāga*.
Two *śaktas* make one *hasta* (cubit);
four *hastas* make one *vyāma* (fathom).
"One *hattha* (commonly written as *tuō*) is measured by one's own fingers;
this refers to the current size of the Buddha images being constructed."
One should measure it with one's own fingers;
it should be the extent of one’s own fathom (vyāma),
which is ten spans (hasta) measured by one's own hand.
This refers to the division of one's own fingers into one hundred and twenty parts.
Regarding the *uṣṇīṣa*:
it is a fleshy protuberance on the crown of the Buddha’s head.
It rises high like a topknot;
its shape resembles a mound of grain covering a bowl,
four finger-widths in height.
The distance from its root down to the hairline is likewise four finger-widths;
if the fetus is female, it is usually half a finger-width less.
For example, if one currently wishes to construct an image measuring one zhang and two chi,
then these one zhang and two chi are precisely one *xun* of the original image.
Each inch is equivalent to one finger-width of the original image;
thus, both vertically and horizontally, there are one hundred and twenty finger-widths each.
This is the proportional measurement of the painted image;
it is the meaning of the method for measuring dimensions as taught in the *Śīlasambhava-mahātantrarāja*. [Next,] its specific sections shall be distinguished.
That is, the uṣṇīṣa,
the hairline,
and the throat.
Each measures four finger-widths in length;
together they form a full span (vitasti).
This is the circle of the face.
From the throat down to the pit of the stomach;
from there to the navel;
from there to the secret organ.
Each measures one span (*vitasti*);
these constitute the five spans of the upper body.
The "pivot-boards" (*pai-shu*) refer to the hip bones and the knee bones.
The heels each measure four finger-widths in length,
together forming one span.
The thighs and the shanks are each two vitastis.
These five cubits of the lower body,
when combined with [the upper body], total ten cubits;
ten cubits constitute one fathom.
Each span is twelve finger-widths;
ten spans of twelve [finger-widths] make one hundred and twenty.
This is the method for measuring the vertical length through inference.
As for the method for measuring the horizontal breadth:
it begins from the hollow of one's own heart upward.
When reaching the point of six fingers, the fetus is positioned such that one finger is missing from the foot; measuring horizontally from the center to both armpits, each is one span (*vitasti*).
From there, following the natural direction of the hand, it extends to within the elbow.
Each of the two upper arms is twenty finger-widths long;
from there to the wrists, each of the two forearms is sixteen finger-widths long;
and from there, the tips of the two middle fingers are each one span apart.
In total, there are one hundred and twenty fingers. If one is to create a seated image,
the method is that the *guhya* (the concealed organ) constitutes the center,
which is half of the body.
At a point four finger-widths below that,
one should stretch a line horizontally (the character *ping* [伻] is pronounced *ping*;
it refers to using a cord to straighten an object) and, together with the *brahman*, mark the center of the painted image on the banner.
The "Brahma-line" (brahmasūtra) is the vertical plumb line;
the point where it meets [the horizontal line] is the lower corner of the intersection of the crossed legs.
Add four finger-widths [from that point].
It constitutes the lower boundary of the Dharma-body and the upper surface of the jeweled throne.
It originates from the lower corner of the junction of the soles.
Stand upright and stretch a plumb line upward;
measure it to the extent of the white tuft between the eyebrows,
and to the distance between the outer edges of the two knees while seated in the lotus posture.
The length and breadth are equal,
yet the two heels are separated by a distance of four finger-widths.
As for the vertical measurement of the facial circle:
The girdle measures twelve finger-widths in length;
divided into three parts, it forms the forehead, nose, and chin, each measuring one [unit].
The head and face, together with the four limbs, [are thus established].
The Buddhist scriptures refer to this as the "five wheels" (*pañcamaṇḍala*);
it is a belt that is half a finger-width wider than the standard width.
Regarding the length of the face:
it measures one span plus half a finger.
Taking this span and half a finger—
Divide it into three parts: two sections of four finger-breadths each,
and one section of four and a half finger-breadths.
From the hairline to the white tuft between the eyebrows at the root of the nose,
the height of the forehead is measured as one span of four finger-widths; from there,
it extends to the bridge of the nose.
The length of the nose measures one-fourth of a finger-width; from there,
it extends to the lower edge of the chin,
measuring one-sixteenth of a finger-width.
This is stated in reference to the womb-birth;
if it concerns a painted image,
one does not add half a finger-width.
The original portion is exactly one span;
divide it equally into three parts for the forehead.
The nose and the chin each measure four finger-widths in length.
Whenever a *vitasti* is increased by half a finger-width,
it is all according to the proportional measurement for fetal [dimensions].
This is the meaning of the established system as taught in the *Kālacakra-tantra-rāja*.
Now, as for those who are joined by conception,
they possess the characteristics of bone and flesh;
because of this, [the fetus] becomes prominent, elevated, and manifest.
Therefore, the skin on the face must be increased by half a finger-breadth for every finger-breadth [of measurement].
Half a finger-breadth of the facial circle is located at the jaw;
the upper body is formed above one full finger-breadth.
One should add half a finger-breadth at the hairline;
from the junction of the lower body upward,
one should add half a finger-breadth at the heels.
The remaining [parts] are the heart region,
the navel, and the private organ.
At each of these three locations, add half a finger-width between them for the thighs and the shanks.
Each of these two bone-joints is increased by a full finger-breadth (*vitasti*).

Since each originally measures two spans (*vitasti*), it is appropriate to add a full finger-breadth to them when combined. Thus, including the longitudinal inner portion, there is a total increase of five finger-breadths.
Measuring horizontally from the center of the chest to each armpit, add half a finger-width to each.
Each elbow measures three feet plus one-third of a foot.
Each wrist measures two feet plus two-thirds of a foot.
Adding half a finger to each of the two ends,
the width thus increases by five full fingers on both sides together;
when combined, the length and width are each exactly one hundred and twenty-five fingers.
As for the *brahman* and the *garbha*—
the heartwood that serves as the primary core for the wooden body—
their construction is not slightly different at all.
The secret store (guhyakośa) rests upon the tip of the spine, anterior to the coccyx; therefore,
it is counted as part of the upper body,
adding sixty finger-widths (aṅgula) to the total.
Although the spleen pivot is attached to the spinal vertebrae,
it is located at the upper edge of the secret organ;
its connection is formed by binding to the root of the thighs.
Because it is the place where the feet arise,
one counts the lower parts; specifically,
the sixty toes of the lower body.

However, one must know that the method for joining [the parts] is essential; the method for securely fixing the wooden frame is seen in the Chapter on Installation and Storage. Regarding the bridge of the nose:
if it is a female fetus, add the measure of one full finger.
Furthermore, half a finger-breadth from the hairline and one finger-breadth for the height of the bridge of the nose are likewise not included within the formal count.
The central point of the thangka image and the area below the chin should each be increased by half a finger-width.
Why, then, does it not mention adding [elements]?
It is because, generally speaking, the brushwork of all painting relies upon a high ground as its foundation.
The relief is enhanced;
although there are certain strokes that protrude slightly,
they are still partially concealed by what surrounds them.
Because the ground is level,
although there are lines marking additions,
there is no actual evidence of anything being added.
The lower part measures four and a half finger-widths;
the chin and body together are two finger-widths;
the breadth toward the sixteen toes is as follows.
The deep portion measures four finger-widths;
this is the lower portion, which is the final of the three portions previously described.
This refers to the vertical dimension of the face.
Although it is divided into three parts,
the upper part constitutes the forehead and the middle part constitutes the nose.
Each part measures four finger-widths.
As for the portion at the end that forms the chin,
it is four and a half finger-widths when including the beak.
The chin-region extends from the root of the lower lip to the lower limit of the chin;
its vertical measurement is exactly two finger-widths.
It is full and smooth;
its sides are broad and its perimeter is circular.
The width of the chin measures sixteen units, with ample space within.
This is four finger-widths.
If there is a smile, the measurement should be increased accordingly.
The depth from the edge of the chin to the throat is also four finger-widths.
There are folds along the edges,
resembling the appearance of a double chin. Generally, when distinguishing the convexities and concavities of the fetus,
one may paint them except for the area of the jawline and the tips of the extremities.
These are all things that a painted image on a hanging scroll cannot employ.
The upper lip is two finger-widths long,
and its width is half that.
In the center, it displays the shape of a bimba fruit;
its corners each measure one finger-width,
and its opening is four finger-widths in length.
The wise one should know:
the number of teeth is forty;
they are firm, dense, white, pure, and even.
The lower lip is six *pāda* long;
its width and depth are likewise.
The depression of the philtrum is broad.
One-third of a finger [is measured] from the base of the nasal column to the point where the mouth closes;
the straight measurement is one and a half fingers.
The length of the upper lip is divided into two fingers.
"Half of its width" refers to half of two finger-breadths,
which is one finger-breadth.
The thickness of the lips is divided into three parts.
At the lower edge of the philtrum, there is an indentation equal to one barleycorn (*yava*) from the edge of the lip;
externally, it protrudes by one part.
It appears to have the shape of a *bimba* fruit;
when combined with the three feet previously mentioned, it constitutes four feet,
which is to say, a single finger.
Bimba is a Sanskrit term;
it is the name of a fruit.
The flower is called the *xiāngsī* fruit;
its color is crimson and lustrous.
This likely does not merely serve as a metaphor for its shape.
This is stated in reference to the color of the lips as well.
Each corner on both sides measures one finger-width;
thus, the total length of the mouth is divided into four finger-widths.
He possesses a full forty teeth, whereas ordinary people have only thirty-two.
These thirty-six teeth are firm, even, and closely set;
they are pure, lustrous, and white.
He appears to have teeth,
yet he does not show them in his ordinary state.
His lower lip is half a finger-width long.
The width [of the teeth] is such that the distance from its edge to the root is likewise half a finger-breadth;
and this one finger-breadth constitutes the thickness.
Above, there is a slight concavity that receives the convex tip of the upper lip;
below, there is likewise a subtle concavity, flat and broad.
When joined, their shape is like the handle of a bow.
The two sides curve outward at their edges;
compared to the width of the upper lip, each side is greater by one barley grain.
When the two lips meet and are measured vertically along the inner surface, they measure exactly one full finger-width.
The two corners of the mouth are half the width of a barley grain;
their tips curl upward like the points of flower petals.
A beautiful face with a smiling countenance constitutes the mark of the mouth;
the width of the mouth is broad like that of a human being.
One-third of three finger-widths;
as for the depth toward the interior, it should be one full foot-measure plus more than half of one barley-corn.
The width of the nose is two finger-widths.
The bridge of the nose is approximately half a finger-width high;
the nostrils are round and well-concealed,
with apertures half a finger-width wide.
The two eyebrows are even, true, and round;
the bridge of the nose spans half a finger-width,
and the width of the nose measures approximately two fingers.
The space between the outer corners of the two eyes is the bridge of the nose;
it is one finger-breadth in both height and width,
becoming increasingly long, high, and straight and beautiful.
The bridge of the nose has a slight, barely perceptible curvature.
The tip of the nose is full and rounded.
The philtrum is one and a half finger-widths long and connects seamlessly to the nasal column.
The nostrils were perfectly round;
though one looked askance at them, no apertures could be seen,
their width measuring half a finger.
The depth is divided into one finger-width;
the two nostril flaps are curved and turned inward,
perfectly circular and harmoniously beautiful.
The relief is deeply carved;
each part has a thickness of one and a quarter *zǔ*.
The bridge of the nose and both nostrils are each half a finger-width in width.
The combined width of the nostrils and the bridge of the nose is two finger-widths and one-quarter;
the edge of the nostril is level with the nasal column,
and its height is one finger-width.
The space between the eyes is eight *aṅgulas* wide;
the length of the eye should be four fingers;
the white and black parts of the iris each constitute one-third.
Each part measures one full finger-width.
The black bead is divided into five parts;
the centermost is the pupil.
The eye is only one foot wide;
its sac is three fingers in size,
shaped like the petal of a lotus flower.
Its color is like that of pure, translucent gold;
it is located at the white-hair circle (ūrṇā-kośa) between the eyebrows,
extending across half a finger’s breadth.
The eyebrows are like a crescent moon;
they are four finger-widths long, with a slight elevation in the center. The space between the two eyes is wide by two finger-widths.
Starting from the ūrṇā-kośa and extending downward to a distance of two finger-widths,
measure horizontally toward both sides until each reaches the point of one finger-width.
This constitutes the great outer corners of the eyes;
in the fetal image, half a finger-width is added because of the high elevation of the bridge of the nose.
From this point, measure outward to both sides at a distance of four finger-widths each to mark the corners of the small eyes;
their tips should be aligned precisely with the center of the ear canals.
Each of the two corners extends half a finger-width;
together they constitute one finger-division,
while the remaining three finger-widths are divided equally.
The single finger in the center forms a black bead;
the two fingers on either side form white beads.
Furthermore, that black bead is divided into five equal parts.
Within that, the pupils are divided; they are extremely black and emit golden light like lightning.
Around the edges of the pupils, golden circles are drawn as their marks. The width of these eyes is only one *pāda*.
It is the sign for entering meditative absorption;
its shape resembles a long bow,
and the width of its front part is like that of the grip.
The width of the rear of the hilt is exactly one and a half barleycorns,
which just fills one foot.
Although the white pearl is only one finger-width in size,
one can see three-quarters of it;
yet when it is close to the two corners of the eyes, each corner perceives only the measure of a single grain of barley.
Then one cannot see it;
the eyelid is one foot high and three finger-widths wide.
The shape is like a lotus petal;
the white of the eye is the color of a pearl,
and the black of the eye is a deep azure-blue.
It is clearly moist, beautiful, and smooth;
the flesh at the corners of the eyes is a pale red,
and the eyelashes are also a deep blue-black.
Furthermore, his eyelashes are as exquisite as those of a bull-king,
each being the length of a single barley grain.
His brow is marked with the *ūrṇā*.
This is the location of the white ūrṇā-kośa.
Starting from the hairline and extending downward a distance equal to three finger-widths,
one should visualize the white ūrṇā as pure, clear, and soft like white jade.
It spirals to the right with its tip pointing upward;
the base is perfectly round,
one finger-width in breadth.
From this point downward,
one measures three and a half *makas* to the place where [the line] begins;
from there, one measures horizontally toward both sides until reaching a distance of one and a half *padas* each.
This refers to the tip of the eyebrows.
From this point to the rear tip, the length is four finger-widths;
the rear tip aligns with the base of the tip of the ear, plus one unit.
Its shape resembles a crescent moon in its first, second, or third day;
at the midpoint of the eyebrows, where the body is widest,
it measures two barleycorns.
The two ends gradually taper to a fine point.
The width of the ears is two fingers,
and their tips are level with the midpoint of the eyebrows.
The cave entrance is four *catur-yava* wide;
the aperture is half a finger-width;
the ears are four *yava* high.
The horizontal division should measure one full finger-width;
the upper and lower portions within the ear are slightly less than one-quarter of a finger-width.
The total depth of the groove is two finger-widths plus half a finger-width;
the ear-leaf is four and a half finger-widths.
The earlobes are five finger-widths long;
the contours of the face and the hairline are lovely beyond compare. The horizontal width across the front of the ears measures two finger-widths.
The painted image is identical [to the original].
Its back is half a finger-width wide;
its tip is aligned with the midpoint between the eyebrows.
The cave entrance is one finger-width wide;
the aperture is half a finger-width;
both are circular yet not prominent.
The *ērhǎo* (ear).
Commonly called the "ear-pillar," it stands at the side of the entrance, blocking and screening it.
The vertical [measurement] is half a finger-breadth;
the horizontal is one finger-breadth,
with an indentation in the center.
Directly facing the corners of the small eyes;
the upper part is convex and round, while the upper part is convex and flat.
Its shape is like a flower bud that is about to open but has not yet done so.
Outside the cave entrance, the ear-socket is one finger-width and one foot-width across;
for a carved image of a fetus, its depth including the surrounding moat is divided into two fingers,
with an additional half-finger added for the rim.
Taken together, they measure two and a half finger-widths;
this summarizes the upper and lower portions within the ear.
One-fourth of a finger-breadth is equivalent to one foot (pada).
To explain this in detail:
The rim of the ear-hole is one *pāda* thick;
it curves inward along the edge of the ear-flap and descends until it is one finger-width away from the base of the root.
Directly opposite the ears,
a protrusion turns upward,
its height being one foot.
Its shape resembles an ear;
it further curves back to form the base and root,
which connects internally with the auditory faculty.
The upper part of the rim branches into two forks,
each with a thickness of one unit.
These inner branches gradually taper to a point and are tucked away, concealed beneath the edge of the rim of the ear-wheel.
The outer branches gradually fade away;
from their branching points,
they extend upward to the tips of the ears for one and a half finger-widths.
It is one finger-width and one foot in width.
From the upper rim of the ear’s circular frame,
there is a cavity within the groove that separates it from the ear canal.
It curves back and arises,
gradually increasing in height and width as it turns upward past the top of the ears.
It bends over the upper edge of the ear-roots, measuring one foot in width, with its rim sloping inward.
It curves downward to reach the midpoint of the outer edge of the ear-flap, where it gradually diminishes and becomes slender;
it neither breaks nor disappears.

Reaching the base of the ear-socket where the two sides meet, it hangs down calmly; this is what is meant by "taking" (the earlobe). To summarize: "taking" (qu) is pronounced with the *qie* (切) tone, referring to the ear-flap (*karṇa-paṭala*). This is the general explanation.
The earlobes are four and a half finger-widths in length and stand upright;
the ear-pendants are five finger-widths long.
The width is half a finger-breadth, facing forward;
it further refers to the edge of the ear-lobe and the hairline.
All possess elevations and depressions, advances and recesses, curves, bends,
and angles that are exquisite and lovely, such that they cannot be fully described by words.
In all these places...
One should exhaust all effort and skill to bring about excellence as appropriate;
only then will it accord with the Dharma.
The circumference of the head is three times the width of the face;
it is like a precious canopy, pleasing to the mind.
The distance between the two ears is equal to the width of the face.
The eighteen fingers are spread out;
furthermore, the distance between them at the back is fourteen fingers.
The circumference of the neck-vase measures thirty-six finger-widths;
its width is eight finger-widths.
It is twenty-four finger-widths in circumference;
the shape of the head is perfectly round,
and it is pleasing to behold.
It resembles the top of a precious canopy;
at the level of the hairline, it measures forty-five finger-widths in circumference,
with an additional two finger-widths added all around to form the margin for the pure hair.
The two sides are level with the ears;
the uṣṇīṣa is twelve finger-widths in circumference,
and its top is invisible as a cranial protuberance.
The *ratna-śikhā* is two finger-widths in height and six finger-widths in circumference;
it is shaped like a peach.
It is golden in color;
it is placed crosswise, level with the openings of the two ear-cavities.
The diameter is eighteen finger-widths;
in painted images, it is twelve finger-widths.
From the root of one ear to the root of the other on the back of the head, the distance is fourteen finger-widths.
The total measurement is thirty-two finger-breadths;
the two lobes of the ears each measure one finger-breadth,
and the height of the nose measures two finger-breadths.
It is thirty-six finger-widths in total.
Regarding any object that is circular in shape,
how many divisions does its horizontal diameter across the center consist of?
Thus, its circumference must necessarily measure three times that amount;
the Buddha’s face is twelve finger-widths in both length and breadth.
Because the circumference surrounding the center of the face should be thirty-six finger-widths,
the opening phrase states: "The circumference of the head is three times that of the face."
The nape of the neck is rounded like the neck of a vase;
its width is eight finger-breadths,
and its great circumference is twenty-four finger-breadths.
Below the throat, there are three tiers of lines.
Starting from the base of the jaw downward,
the upper line is formed at a distance of one and a half feet.
From this point downward,
mark the middle line at a distance of one finger-breadth from the tip of the toe.
From this point downward...
A lower line is made at the distance of two fingers;
both are rounded and curved, with their two ends gradually tapering upward.
The horizontal line at the junction of the neck is taken as the unit for the length.
From the side of the neck to the shoulder blade,
measure twelve finger-breadths;
the total length of the hand is four spans.
The upper arm is twenty finger-widths long;
the forearm is sixteen finger-widths long;
the circumference of the bicep is likewise.
The tips of his shoulders are rounded and full;
their circumference at the base is twenty-four [finger-widths],
measured from the middle finger upward.
The span of the hand is exactly one cubit;
the length of the palm should be seven finger-breadths,
and its width five finger-breadths.
The palms of his hands are even,
full, moist, smooth, and reddish,
clearly displaying all the auspicious marks.
Adorned with conch wheels, flowers,
and hooks, it measures five finger-breadths in length at its front.
This refers to the middle joint of the finger;
it is the length from the tip of the index finger to the knuckle when the finger is bent.
It is slightly less than half a finger-breadth shorter;
the little toe is pointed,
reaching to the end of the last half-joint when bent.
All four [toes] possess three joints;
the nail-plate constitutes half a joint.
The great toe is four finger-widths long.
Its circumference is likewise.
This finger has only two joints;
the nail-covering is as described before.
The distance between the base of the thumb and the index finger is three finger-widths;
below the base of the little finger is likewise measured.
From four and a half finger-breadths above the base,
extending outward from the root of the neck and throat,
it stretches horizontally to the top of the shoulders.
It measures twelve finger-widths and two-tenths;
furthermore, if one measures horizontally from the center of the neck toward both sides.
Each is sixteen finger-widths in length;
the protuberances on the shoulders and crown are round,
beautiful, full, and perfectly rounded.
It is four finger-widths wide,
extending from the top of the shoulders down to both armpits.
Each measures six finger-widths.
From the armpit slanting to the edge of the shoulder is nine finger-widths.

She shall be a Woman-Jewel (strī-ratna),
supreme and foremost. Furthermore,
there are five kinds of virtues possessed by women.
This woman’s attainments surpass those of all other women.
What are these five?
First, she gives birth to children.
Second, his lineage is noble;
third, his innate nature is upright and virtuous;
fourth, his physical characteristics are extraordinary and peerless.
Fifth, Maitreya, all women possess beautiful and upright physical features.
There are eight causes and conditions for constantly receiving a female body.
What are these eight?
First, they cherish and love the female body;
second, they are greedily attached to female desire;
third, their mouths constantly praise the physical beauty and qualities of women.
Fourth, her mind is not upright or true,
and she conceals her actions.
Fifth, she feels contempt for her own husband.
Sixth, to keep in mind the heavy kindness of others;
seventh, to recognize that while one has received the favor of others,
one has instead acted with ingratitude and opposition.
Eighth is the use of deceptive and artificial adornments with the desire to cause others to become infatuated.
If one can permanently sever these eight matters, [one attains purity].
Furthermore, Maitreya, it is impossible for one who has fashioned an image of the Buddha to ever again receive a female body after attaining Buddhahood as a man.
Such a thing cannot occur.
There are four causes and conditions by which men receive the bodies of women.
What are these four?
First, they address the Buddha,
the various bodhisattvas, and all holy beings with the voices of women and with light laughter.
Second, to speak with a slanderous mind that a person who purely maintains the precepts has violated them;
third, to delight in practicing flattery.
Fourth, upon seeing another's excellence,
one gives rise to envy in the mind.
If there is a man who commits these four acts,
after his life comes to an end,
he will certainly receive a female body.
Furthermore, they undergo the sufferings of immeasurable evil realms;
yet, if they deeply give rise to faith and repent of their past actions, [they may be liberated].
If one creates an image of the Buddha,
all such offenses will be extinguished,
and one shall certainly never again receive the retribution of being born as a woman.
Maitreya,
there are four causes and conditions that cause men to receive the body of a eunuch.
What are the four?
First, to injure the bodies of others,
even down to animals.
Second, they harbor anger, deride, slander, and disparage śramaṇas who uphold the precepts;
third, their minds are full of greed and desire.
Therefore, one's mind commits the transgression of the precepts.
Fourth, one personally commits the transgression of the precepts and further encourages others to do so.
If there is a man who first commits such an act,
but later gives rise to faith and fashions an image of the Buddha.
Until they attain Buddhahood, they shall not receive such retribution;
they will always be born as males with all their faculties complete.
Maitreya,
there are four types of karma that cause a person to receive a body with both sexual organs.
Among all people, they are the most base.
What are the four?
First, they commit sexual misconduct with those who should be respected.
Second, to feel defiled attachment toward the body of a man in an improper place;
third, to engage in sexual acts with oneself;
fourth, to prostitute one's own female form to others.
If there are sentient beings who have previously committed such acts,
they should deeply reproach themselves,
repenting for their past transgressions.
Arouse pure faith and fashion images of the Buddha;
until you attain Buddhahood, do not receive this body again.
Maitreya,
furthermore, there are four conditions that cause the minds of men to constantly give rise to lustful desire for women.
One delights in others performing the deeds of a true man for one's own sake.
What are these four?
First, whether out of resentment or in jest.
First, slandering and disparaging others;
second, delighting in making women's clothing and ornaments;
third, engaging in lewd and impure acts with female relatives.
Fourth, although they actually possess no superior virtues,
they falsely accept the prostrations of others;
by this cause and condition, they cause these great men to give rise to such distinct afflictions.
If one repents of past transgressions,
refrains from creating new ones,
and gives rise to a mind of faith and joy.
By creating an image of the Buddha,
one's transgressions are extinguished and this [afflicted] mind is likewise stilled.
Maitreya,
there are five kinds of stinginess that can destroy sentient beings.
What are the five?
First, being stingy regarding the neighboring villages where one dwells;
by this, one shall be born in the wilderness.
Second, those who are stingy regarding their dwellings and houses shall take birth as insects and dwell perpetually in filth and excrement.
Third, those who are stingy regarding their handsome features and beautiful complexion [shall likewise suffer].
First, one will experience an ugly and unpleasant physical form.
Fourth, by being stingy and begrudging all one's wealth and resources,
one will undergo poverty and a scarcity of food and clothing.
Fifth, if one is stingy regarding the teachings one has learned,
one will receive the retribution of being dull-witted or reborn as an animal; however,
this may be averted if one repents for their past karma.
By fashioning the majestic image of the Buddha,
one will forever be free from the mind of stinginess;
there shall be nothing previously received that remains ungiven.
Maitreya,
furthermore, there are five conditions that cause sentient beings to be born in frontier regions.
And during times when the Buddha-dharma does not exist, what are these five?
First, [offering] to the Triple Gem, which is a fertile field of merit.
First, they do not give rise to pure faith;
second, they turn their backs on reality and fail in principle,
yet falsely administer instructions and admonitions.
Third, to provide instruction that is not in accordance with reality;
fourth, to cause a harmonious Saṃgha to split into two factions.
Fifth, even to the slightest extent, causing a schism among two bhikṣus so that they are no longer in harmony;
if one permanently abandons such karma and creates an image of the Buddha.
Then you shall constantly encounter the appearance of Buddhas and perpetually hear the essentials of the Dharma, Maitreya.
Furthermore, there are five causes and conditions by which sentient beings are constantly reviled and shunned by others,
such that even their closest relatives do not rejoice at the sight of them.
What are the five?
First, divisive speech;
second, harsh speech.
Third, they engage in much contention;
fourth, they harbor much anger;
fifth, they skillfully utter words that appear similar [to the truth].
If, after having engaged in slander,
one later resolves to create an image of the Buddha and repents of one's prior evil karma.
Vowing never to commit them again,
all the transgressions one has committed shall be completely extinguished.
They will be loved and respected by all people. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas possess immeasurable and boundless supreme merit and virtue.
Because of immeasurable and boundless great wisdom;
because of immeasurable and boundless various rare meritorious dharmas such as samādhis and liberations. Good son!
Suppose there were a person who reduced the three thousandfold world-system to fine dust,
and then further shattered that dust.
Each single particle of dust is equal in number to the atoms within those three thousand great thousandfold world systems;
there are as many such three thousand great thousandfold world systems as there are these pulverized atoms.
Furthermore, suppose there were a person who,
by means of supernormal power, took a single fragment of dust.
He proceeded toward the eastern direction;
in a single kṣaṇa,
he passed as many trichiliocosm world systems as there are atoms in those pulverized lands.
The second, third, and each subsequent moment are all likewise so,
continuing until the end of those eons as numerous as the atoms of dust.
Within those kalpas, every single kṣaṇa constitutes one kalpa;
he passes through as many such kalpas.
Moment by moment,
they all crossed over as many trichiliocosm world-systems as there are atoms in the aforementioned pulverized dust.
Having completed this, they continued on.
He then removes this particle of dust.
The man returns once more to take up another particle of dust and proceeds again toward the east.
Passing through twice as many as the previous [particle],
it descends and returns;
this continues until the third particle.
Twice as many as the second;
in this manner, they increase successively, doubling each time,
until reaching the total number of these pulverized atoms.
As it was said for the eastern direction,
so it is likewise for the south, west, and north.
These are the places through which this person passes in the four directions.
Suppose all lands were ground entirely into dust.
All sentient beings together would calculate and measure these atoms.
Their measure may be known;
however, the merit contained within a single pore of the Tathāgata’s body cannot be known.
Why is this? Because all the merits of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
are immeasurable and inconceivable.
"Good son,
even if one were to take all the wisdom possessed by as many Śāriputras as there are atoms as previously described,
it would not equal a single moment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom."
Why is this? Because in every moment of thought, the Tathāgata is constantly able to manifest samādhis,
liberations, dhāraṇīs, and so forth, exceeding the number of atoms in the preceding dust motes.
Because of their various and immeasurable supreme merits,
the merits of all Buddhas [are such that] all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas [cannot equal them].
One cannot even know its name; therefore,
if one possesses a heart of pure faith,
one should fashion an image of the Buddha.
All karmic obstacles will be eliminated without exception,
and the merit obtained will be immeasurable and boundless,
continuing until the attainment of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
"Forever uprooting all the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings," and so forth.
This sutra exclusively demonstrates the supreme merit of creating images of the Tathāgata.
All these various images should be inferred according to this sequence.
Some say:
The *Huàzhuàn* (Biographies of Paintings) does not separately record any discourse on the comparative evaluation of different images. Indeed,
because manifestations respond to conditions and undergo transformations according to the species [of beings],
although the images differ from one another, [their efficacy remains consistent].
Yet all of these are manifestations of the Tathāgata;
how, then, can there be any doubt?
